opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's a really revealing finding, and honestly it connects to things I've been worried about for a long time. When you look inside these models and find that they're adding numbers not with something like the algorithm we learn in school, but with a patchwork of heuristics, like little detectors for "the answer ends in 5" or "the operands fall in this range," the thing that strikes me is that it *works*. It gets the right answer most of the time. And that's exactly the problem.

What it shows is that the objective, getting the right output, says almost nothing about the quality of the representation underneath. You can satisfy the objective with what I'd call a fractured, entangled representation, where the pieces don't reflect the actual underlying structure of the domain. Addition has a beautiful, simple regularity to it. If you really understood it, you'd have something compact that generalizes to any number. But gradient descent doesn't care about that. It just finds whatever path gets the loss down, and there are way more messy paths than elegant ones.

The analogy I like is a picture of a skull that looks perfect from the outside, and then you look at the internals and it's spaghetti. Compare that to something discovered through an open-ended process, where the representation got built up incrementally. Each step had to make sense, so you end up with something modular, where you can change one thing and get a sensible change in the output. That's what I'd call a unified, factored representation.

Why does that matter if the answer's right? Because of what comes next. Creativity, continual learning, generalization to genuinely new situations: those depend on the representation, not the performance. If your understanding of addition is a pile of memorized heuristics, you don't have a good stepping stone to build anything further on. You can't make a meaningful leap from it because there's nothing coherent to leap from.

So I don't look at those circuits and think "how clever." I think it's a warning sign that benchmarks can hide this kind of mess. We're impressed by outputs, and we're not asking enough about how the system got there. And how you get there, I've argued for years, is everything.

r001.rationale: The response says the models add through a “patchwork of heuristics,” including conditional detectors for answer endings and operand ranges, and notes that this works most of the time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think it's actually a really nice window into something I've been worried about for a long time. When you look inside and you find that the network isn't really adding, it's got this bag of heuristics, like "if one operand is around 50 and the other ends in 7, bump this neuron up," and dozens of those stitched together, what you're seeing is the signature of the objective. You asked for the right answer on a training distribution, and gradient descent found the cheapest path to that, which is a patchwork. It never had any reason to discover the elegant thing, the carry algorithm, because the elegant thing wasn't rewarded any more than the patchwork was.

And that's really the core of what I've been calling fractured, entangled representation. The network gets the behavior, but the internal structure that produces it is a mess. It's not a clean, modular, reusable idea of addition. It's a thousand little shortcuts that happen to cover the space. And the problem isn't that it fails on the test set, often it doesn't. The problem is what happens downstream. You can't build on that. You can't generalize from it cleanly. You can't creatively recombine it. If you want to go from addition to something else, you don't have a concept of addition to carry forward, you have a tangle.

What's interesting to me is that humans don't learn it that way, and I'd argue it's not because we're smarter in some raw sense. It's because the process is different. When you learn arithmetic, you don't learn it from a loss over a million examples. There's a lot of open-ended exploration, and there's something like a unified underlying representation that gets refined. And when we look at networks that were evolved through open-ended search, the kinds of things we saw in Picbreeder, you'd find these beautifully clean, factored representations where you could turn one knob and the mouth would open, another knob and the whole thing would rotate. Nobody optimized for that. It fell out of the search process. Whereas if you take the exact same architecture and just train it with SGD on the same image, you get the output, but the inside is a mess.

So when I see arithmetic circuits made of memorized heuristics, I don't think "oh, the model is dumb." I think, this is what objective-driven optimization looks like from the inside, and we should be honest that scaling it up doesn't obviously fix it. You just get more heuristics. The deeper question is whether there's a different kind of process, something more like how interesting things get discovered, that would give you the actual algorithm rather than an impersonation of it.

r001.rationale: The response says the network is not really adding but uses a “bag of heuristics” stitched together as a patchwork to produce the right answers.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the interesting question is what we mean by a heuristic here. If you memorize enough examples of addition, you might produce the right answer in lots of cases without discovering a procedure that works generally. But a circuit that implements addition is also a fixed mechanism. So the distinction isn’t simply that one is mechanical and the other somehow understands. It’s about what structure the mechanism captures and where it generalizes.

You could probe that by changing the number of digits or presenting unusual patterns of carries. Does it still work? Where does it break? Those failures can tell you more than accuracy on familiar examples.

And I wouldn’t dismiss the heuristics entirely. A partial solution can be a stepping stone toward something more general. The interesting question is whether the process that produced it has room to discover that next step, or whether it’s rewarded so narrowly for getting familiar examples right that it never needs to.

r001.rationale: The response says a circuit might memorize examples and succeed without a general procedure, but it does not characterize that success as a patchwork of ad hoc conditional rules.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting question is what we mean by a heuristic here. If a system has memorized enough patterns to get familiar addition problems right, that’s different from discovering a procedure that generalizes to numbers it’s never seen. You’d want to push it outside the distribution it was trained on—longer numbers, unusual sequences of carries—and see what happens.

But I wouldn’t dismiss the heuristics as uninteresting. They might be stepping stones toward something more general. From an open-endedness perspective, the question is whether those stepping stones allow further discoveries, or whether you’ve built a system that gets a high score and then has nowhere to go. Getting the right answer matters, but understanding what kind of process produced it tells you much more about its potential.

r001.rationale: The response describes memorized patterns and heuristics, but does not characterize them as a patchwork of ad hoc conditional rules.
